regions: Central Asia, Siberia and the steppe
early: Stone tools - found in modern-day Kenya are older
Ancient stone tools from Ethiopia (Oldowan) were hand-crafted by Australopithecus
Advanced (Acheulean) stone tools in Kenya by Homo erectus
Africa (the page names Homo erectus but no place)
Earliest likely control of fire by Homo Erectus
Cooking in Middle East by Homo erectus
Hafting (fixing a stone point to a handle)
Hafting in South Africa by Homo heidelbergensis
Schöningen Spears in Germany likely by Homo heidelbergensis or early Neandarthals
Simple glue (adhesive) made of one kind of material, birch tar, in Central Italy by Neanderthals
Clothing, among anatomically modern humans in Africa
Harpoons in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Arrows and other evidence of bow-and-arrow technology
Sewing needle (implying thread of some kind)
Earliest evidence of a sewing needle, made and used by Denisovans
fragments of an axe in Australia date to 49-45 ka
The oldest-known mines in the world are from Eswatini
Tally sticks (see Lebombo bone) in Eswatini
Oldest known pottery, used to make figurines rather than cooking or storage vessels (Venus of Dolní Věstonice)
Earliest pottery use, in Xianren Cave, China
The oldest spear-thrower (aka atlatl, woomera) found so far was in France
Domestication of the dog in Siberia
The oldest agreed domestic dog remains belongs to the Bonn-Oberkassel dog
Fish hook in Okinawa Island, modern day Japan
Spindle whorl, also the oldest wheel-like tool, at Nahal Ein Gev II, Israel
dated from 10,000 to 8,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent
Rice was domesticated in this region ... between 13,500 and 8,200 years ago
It was the domestication centre for foxtail millet (Setaria italica) and broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), with early evidence of domestication approximately 8,000 years ago
Kuk Swamp, New Guinea Highlands (taro, bananas)
perhaps 8000 BCE in the Kuk Early Agricultural Site of Papua New Guinea
squash as early as 6000 BCE, beans no later than 4000 BCE, and maize beginning about 7000 BCE
The Indigenous peoples of the southwestern Amazon basin domesticate cassava, the first domestic crop in the New World
Domestication of potatoes, in southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia ... around Lake Titicaca
three areas have been identified as having independently developed agriculture: the Ethiopian highlands, the Sahel and West Africa
Crops domesticated in the Sahel region include sorghum and pearl millet
West Africa (African rice, yams, oil palm)
Other crops domesticated in West Africa include African rice, yams and the oil palm
In what is now the eastern United States, Native Americans domesticated sunflower, sumpweed and goosefoot c. 2500 BCE
Fertile Crescent (goats, sheep, pigs, taurine cattle)
In the Fertile Crescent 11,000 to 10,000 years ago ... goats, pigs, sheep, and taurine cattle were the first livestock to be domesticated
Two thousand years later, humped zebu cattle were domesticated in what is today Baluchistan in Pakistan
In East Asia 8,000 years ago, pigs were domesticated from wild boar genetically different from those found in the Fertile Crescent
The cat was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, perhaps 10,000 years ago
Alcohol fermentation, specifically mead, in Southwest Asia
Mudbricks (unfired bricks), and clay mortar in Jericho
Oldest known water well in Cyprus
The Pesse canoe is the oldest boat we have found
Sled dog and Dog sled, in Siberia
Great Lakes, North America (Old Copper Complex tools)
Copper tools, by the people of the Old Copper Complex from the Great Lakes region of North America
Copper smelting in evidence in Pločnik and Belovode
Evidence of lead smelting in Çatalhöyük, Turkey
Oldest evidence of cheese found, in Poland and on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia
Oldest evidence of cheese found, in Poland and on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia
Sailing, pottery depictions of sail boats, in Mesopotamia
Cotton thread, in Mehrgarh, Indus Valley
Lost-wax casting in Palestine or the Indus Valley
Lost-wax casting in Palestine or the Indus Valley
Paved roads, in and around the Mesopotamian city of Ur, Iraq
The earliest pipes were made of clay, and are found at the Temple of Bel at Nippur in Babylonia
Oldest evidence of locks, the earliest example discovered in the ruins of Nineveh
North of the Black Sea (miniature clay wheels)
The oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement was found in the form of miniature clay wheels north of the Black Sea before 4000 BCE
depictions of wheeled wagons found on clay tablet pictographs at the Eanna district of Uruk ... dated to c. 3500 to 3350 BCE
Depictions of a wheeled vehicle appeared between 3631 and 3380 BCE in the Bronocice clay pot
with the oldest find in Northern Germany dating back to around 3400 BCE
The Ljubljana Marshes Wheel with axle, the oldest wooden wheel yet discovered, dating to the Copper Age (c. 3130 BCE)
Potter's wheels are thought to have been used in the 4th millennium BCE in the Middle East. The oldest surviving example ... Ur
The earliest known examples of wooden spoked wheels are from the Sintashta culture, dating to c. 2000 BCE
Probable first domestication of the horse in the Eurasian Steppes
Ploughing, on a site in Bubeneč, Czech Republic
Evidence, c. 2800 BC, has also been found at Kalibangan, Indus Valley
Pločnik, Serbia (tin bronze foil, dating disputed)
earliest tin-alloy bronze was a foil dated to the mid-5th millennium BC from a Vinča culture site in Pločnik, Serbia
Bronze was independently discovered in the Maykop culture of the North Caucasus as early as the mid-4th millennium BC
West Asia and the Near East were the first regions to enter the Bronze Age, beginning with the rise of the Mesopotamian civilization of Sumer in the mid-4th millennium BC
Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs both gradually evolved from proto-writing between 3400 and 3100 BC
symbols inscribed between 3400 and 3200 BC were discovered at Abydos
The earliest attested Chinese characters comprise the body of inscriptions on oracle bones and bronze vessels dating to the Late Shang period ... with the earliest of these dated c. 1250 BC
The earliest inscriptions identifiable as Maya date to the 3rd century BC
The first documented swords. They have been found in Arslantepe, Turkey
the oldest known dice ... were excavated as part of a backgammon-like game set at the Burnt City
Prosthesis first documented in the Ancient Near East, in ancient Egypt and Iran
the eye found in Iran was likely made of bitumen paste
The Ruler, or Measuring rod, in the subdivided Nippur, copper rod
Public sewage and sanitation systems in Indus Valley sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Rakhigarhi
Balance weights and scales, from the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt
Fork in Bronze Age Qijia culture in China
Water clock by at least the old Babylonian period ... but possibly earlier from Mohenjo-Daro in the Indus Valley
possibly earlier from Mohenjo-Daro in the Indus Valley
The first alphabetic writing was developed by workers in the Sinai Peninsula to write West Semitic languages c. 1800 BC
Greek alphabet, the first with vowels
The Greek alphabet was the first to use dedicated letters for writing vowels
Sundial in Ancient Egypt or Babylonia
Sundial in Ancient Egypt or Babylonia
Glass manufacture in either Mesopotamia or Ancient Egypt
Glass manufacture in either Mesopotamia or Ancient Egypt
Distillation is described on Akkadian tablets documenting perfumery operations
Saddle (fringed cloths or pads used by Assyrian cavalry)
Coins in Phoenicia (Modern Lebanon) or Lydia
Coins in Phoenicia (Modern Lebanon) or Lydia
Wagonway called Diolkos across the Isthmus of Corinth in Ancient Greece
Crank motion (rotary quern) in Carthage or 5th century BC Celtiberian Spain
Crank motion (rotary quern) in Carthage or 5th century BC Celtiberian Spain
High Carbon Steel, produced by the Closed Crucible method, later known as Wootz steel, of South India
Systematization of medicine and surgery in the Sushruta Samhita in Vedic Northern India
the earliest cast iron is developed in China by the early 5th century BC ... the oldest specimens found in a tomb of Luhe County in Jiangsu province
Catapult by Ajatashatru in Magadha, India
Camera obscura described by Mo-tzu (or Mozi) in China
Invention of the concept of zero in Babylon (now Iraq). It was invented independently by the Maya in the first few centuries AD
It was invented independently by the Maya in the first few centuries AD
Zero and its operation are first defined by (Hindu astronomer and mathematician) Brahmagupta in 628
With decimal place-value and a symbol for zero ... developed in the Indian subcontinent between the 1st and 6th centuries CE
Nailed horseshoe, with 4 bronze shoes found in an Etruscan tomb
Analog computers in the Hellenistic world (see e.g. the Antikythera mechanism), possibly in Rhodes
Archimedes' screw ... was first used in the Nile river for irrigation purposes in Ancient Egypt
Canal lock in Canal of the Pharaohs under Ptolemy II
Indian Pali texts dating to the 4th century BCE refer to the cakkavattaka
Helaine Selin suggests that the device existed in Persia before 350 BC
The clearest description of the water wheel ... is provided by Philo of Byzantium
Paper in Han dynasty China (2nd century BC); Paper was invented in China during the 2nd century AD, and is traditionally credited to Cai Lun
Astrolabe invented by Apollonius of Perga
The aeolipile, a simple steam turbine is recorded by Hero of Alexandria
Seismometer and pendulum in Han dynasty China, built by Zhang Heng
Woodblock printing is invented in Han dynasty China at sometime before 220 AD
The process of producing crystallised sugar from sugar cane, in India, dates to at least the beginning of the common era
Simple suspension bridge, independently invented in Pre-Columbian South America, and the Hindu Kush range
Simple suspension bridge, independently invented in Pre-Columbian South America, and the Hindu Kush range
The horse collar as a fully developed collar harness is developed in Northern and Southern dynasties China during the 5th century AD
Charkha (spinning wheel/cotton gin) invented in India (probably during the Vakataka dynasty of Maharashtra, India), between 500 and 1000 A.D.
Toilet paper in Sui dynasty China
Toothbrush in China during the Tang dynasty
Greek fire in Constantinople, Byzantine Empire
The banknote is first developed in China during the Tang and Song dynasties, starting in the 7th century
True porcelain is manufactured in northern China from roughly the beginning of the Tang dynasty in the 7th century
Gunpowder is, according to prevailing academic consensus, discovered in the 9th century by Chinese alchemists
Playing card in Tang dynasty China
Algebra (al-Khwarizmi's text) and Indian arithmetic in the Islamic world

Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi played a significant role in the development of algebra, arithmetic and Hindu-Arabic numerals; The first true algebra text which is still extant is the work on al-jabr and al-muqabala by Mohammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, written in Baghdad around 825
Fire lance is the earliest firearm in the world
Fountain pen: invented at the request of al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah in Arab Egypt
The first record of a movable type system is in the Dream Pool Essays, which attributes the invention of the movable type to Bi Sheng
The earliest hand cannon dates to the 13th century based on archaeological evidence from a Heilongjiang excavation
Printing press in Mainz, Germany: The printing press is invented in the Holy Roman Empire by Johannes Gutenberg before 1440
tl: Floating dry dock in Venice, Venetian Republic
Mercator Projection map created by Gerardus Mercator
Stocking frame: Invented by William Lee.
Backstaff: Invented by Captain John Davis
Newspaper (Relation): Johann Carolus in Strassburg (see also List of the oldest newspapers)

Telescope: Patent applied for by Hans Lippershey. Actual inventor unknown since it seemed to already be a common item being offered by the spectacle makers in the Netherlands with Jacob Metius also applying for patent and the son of Zacharias Janssen making a claim 47 years later that his father invented it.

Compound microscopes, which combine an objective lens with an eyepiece to view a real image, first appear in Europe. Apparently derived from the telescope, actual inventor unknown, variously attributed to Zacharias Janssen (his son claiming it was invented in 1590), Cornelis Drebbel, and Galileo Galilei.
Slide rule: invented by William Oughtred
Mechanical calculator. The Pascaline is built by Blaise Pascal.
Barometer: invented by Evangelista Torricelli, or possibly up to three years earlier by Gasparo Berti.
Vacuum pump: Invented by Otto von Guericke.
Pendulum clock: Invented by Christiaan Huygens. It was first conceptualized in 1637 by Galileo Galilei but he was unable to create a working model.
First functional reflecting telescope constructed by Isaac Newton.
Christiaan Huygens provides the first known description of a piston engine.
Thomas Savery develops a steam-powered water pump: for draining mines
Bartolomeo Cristofori crafts the first piano, which became a leading instrument of Western art music
Thomas Newcomen builds the first commercial steam engine to pump water out of mines.
Lewis Paul and John Wyatt invent the first mechanized cotton spinning machine, helping to establish the British textile industry
Musschenbroek and Kleist independently develop the Leyden jar, an early form of capacitor.
John Roebuck invents the lead chamber process, mass producing sulfuric acid for manufacturing
William Cullen invents the first artificial refrigeration machine
James Hargreaves invents the spinning jenny, revolutionizing textile production during the Industrial Revolution
Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot invents the first steam-powered vehicle capable of carrying passengers, an early car
John Wilkinson invents his boring machine, considered by some to be the first machine tool
Jesse Ramsden invents the modern screw-cutting lathe
John Wilkinson invents a mechanical air compressor that would become the prototype for all later mechanical compressors
Hyder Ali of Mysore, India develops the first metal-cylinder rockets.
Claude de Jouffroy builds the first steamboat
Joseph-Ralf and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier build the first manned hot air balloon
Louis-Sébastien Lenormand invents and uses the first modern parachute
Martinus van Marum is the first to use the electrolysis technique
Andrew Meikle invents the threshing machine
Edmund Cartwright invents the power loom
Claude Chappe invents the semaphore telegraph
Eli Whitney invents the modern cotton gin
Joseph Bramah invents the hydraulic press
Alois Senefelder invents the lithography printing technique.
Edward Jenner invented the vaccine and inoculates an individual for smallpox
The first paper machine is invented by Louis-Nicolas Robert
Alessandro Volta invents the voltaic pile, an early form of battery in Italy, based on previous works by Luigi Galvani.
Humphry Davy invents the arc lamp (exact date unclear; not practical as a light source until the invention of efficient electric generators).
Friedrich Sertürner discovers morphine as the first active alkaloid extracted from the opium poppy plant.
Joseph Marie Jacquard develops his automated Jacquard loom.
Richard Trevithick invents the steam locomotive.
Hanaoka Seishū creates tsūsensan, the first modern general anesthetic.
Nicéphore Niépce invents  an early internal combustion engine capable of doing useful work.
François Isaac de Rivaz designs the first automobile powered by an internal combustion engine fuelled by hydrogen.
Robert Fulton expands water transportation and trade with the workable steamboat.
Nicolas Appert invents the canning process for food.
Abraham-Louis Breguet creates the first wristwatch.
Friedrich Koenig invents the first powered printing press, which was also the first to use a cylinder.
William Reid Clanny pioneered the invention of the safety lamp which he improved in later years. Safety lamps based on Clanny's improved design were used until the adoption of electric lamps.
James Fox invents the modern planing machine, though Matthew Murray of Leeds and Richard Roberts of Manchester have also been credited at times with its invention.
René Laennec  invents the first Stethoscope.
Francis Ronalds builds the first working electric telegraph using electrostatic means.
Robert Stirling invents the Stirling engine.
Baron Karl von Drais invents the dandy horse, an early velocipede and precursor to the modern bicycle.
Marc Isambard Brunel invents the tunnelling shield.
Thomas Blanchard invents the pattern-tracing lathe (actually more like a shaper). The lathe can copy symmetrical shapes and is used for making gun stocks, and later, ax handles.
Nicéphore Niépce invents Heliography, the first photographic process.
Charles Babbage, considered the "father of the computer", begins building the first programmable mechanical computer.
Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner invents the first lighter.
Johann Nikolaus von Dreyse invents the bolt-action rifle.
John Walker invents the friction match.
James Sharp invents and goes on to manufacture the first practical gas stove.
James Beaumont Neilson develops the hot blast process.
Patrick Bell invents the reaping machine.
Hungarian physicist Ányos Jedlik invents the first commutated rotary electromechanical machine with electromagnets.
Louis Braille invents the Braille reading system for the blind.
William Mann invents the compound air compressor.
Henry Robinson Palmer is awarded a patent for corrugated galvanised iron.
Edwin Budding invents the lawn mower.

Michael Faraday invents a method of electromagnetic induction. It would be independently invented by Joseph Henry the following year. Faraday is credited with inventing the first electric generator called the Faraday disk.
Charles Babbage introduces his "mechanical calculating machine", the first mechanical computer
Moritz von Jacobi invents the first practical electric motor.
Joseph Henry invents the electromechanical relay.
William Otis invents the steam shovel.
James Nasmyth invents the steam hammer.
Edmond Becquerel invents a method for the photovoltaic effect, effectively producing the first solar cell.
Kirkpatrick Macmillan invents the first bicycle
Alexander Bain devises a printing telegraph.
William Robert Grove invents the first fuel cell.
John Bennet Lawes invents superphosphate, the first man-made fertilizer.
Friedrich Gottlob Keller and, independently, Charles Fenerty come up with the wood pulp method of paper production.
Francis Rynd invents the hypodermic needle.
Horace Wells successfully used nitrous oxide as an anesthesia
Isaac Charles Johnson invents modern Portland cement.
Henri-Joseph Maus invents the tunnel boring machine.
Elias Howe received a patent for a sewing machine, the model for the Singer Sewing Machine
Ascanio Sobrero invents nitroglycerin, the first explosive made that was stronger than black powder.
Jonathan J. Couch invents the pneumatic drill.
Linus Yale Sr. invents the first modern pin tumbler lock.
Walter Hunt invents the first repeating rifle to use metallic cartridges (of his own design) and a spring-fed magazine.
James B. Francis invents the Francis turbine.
Walter Hunt invents the safety pin.
William Armstrong invents the hydraulic accumulator.

George Jennings offers the first public flush toilets, accessible for a penny per visit, and in 1852 receives a UK patent for the single piece, free standing, earthenware, trap plumed, flushing, water-closet.
Robert Bunsen is the first to use a chemical vapor deposition technique.
Elisha Otis invents the safety brake elevator.
Henri Giffard becomes the first person to make a manned, controlled and powered flight using a dirigible.
James Clerk Maxwell invents the first practical method for color photography, whether chemical or electronic.
Henry Bessemer patents the Bessemer process for making steel, with improvements made by others over the following years.
Alexander Parkes invents parkesine, also known as celluloid, the first man-made plastic.
James Harrison produces the world's first practical ice making machine and refrigerator using the principle of vapour compression in Geelong, Australia.
William Henry Perkin invents mauveine, the first synthetic dye.
Heinrich Geissler invents the Geissler tube.
The phonautograph, the earliest known device for recording sound, is patented and invented by Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville.
Gaston Planté invents the lead acid battery, the first rechargeable battery.
Richard Jordan Gatling invents the Gatling gun, the first multi-barrel rapid-fire gun.
Louis Pasteur invents the pasteurization process.
Carl Wilhelm Siemens and Pierre-Émile Martin invent the Siemens-Martin process for making steel.
Alfred Nobel invents dynamite, the first safely manageable explosive stronger than black powder.
Lucien B. Smith invents barbed wire.
Polyvinyl chloride, more commonly known as vinyl, is synthesized by German chemist Eugen Baumann.
J. E. T. Woods and J. Clark invent stainless steel. Harry Brearley is the first to commercialize it.
Frederick Ransome invents the rotary kiln.
William Crookes, a chemist, invents the Crookes radiometer as the by-product of some chemical research.
Zénobe Gramme invents the first commercial electrical generator, the Gramme machine.
Gustave Trouvé invents the first metal detector.
Ferdinand von Zeppelin invents the Zeppelin rigid airship.
Fyodor Pirotsky invents the first electric tram near Saint Petersburg, Russia.
Nicolaus August Otto invents the four-stroke cycle.
Alexander Graham Bell has a patent granted for the telephone. However, other inventors before Bell had worked on the development of the telephone and the invention had several pioneers.
Thomas Edison invents the first working phonograph.
Henry Fleuss is granted a patent for the first practical rebreather.
Lester Allan Pelton invents the Pelton wheel, a type of water turbine.

Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison both patent a functional incandescent light bulb. Some two dozen inventors had experimented with electric incandescent lighting over the first three-quarters of the 19th century but never came up with a practical design. Swan's, which he had been working on since the 1860s, had a low resistance so was only suited for small installations. Edison designed a high-resistance bulb as part of a large-scale commercial electric lighting utility.
Nikolay Benardos presents carbon arc welding, the first practical arc welding method.
Hiram Maxim invents the recoil-operated Maxim gun, ushering in the age of semi- and fully automatic firearms.
Paul Vieille invents Poudre B, the first smokeless powder for firearms.
Sir Charles Parsons invents the modern steam turbine.
Hungarian engineers Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri invent the closed core high efficiency transformer and the AC parallel power distribution.
John Kemp Starley invents the modern safety bicycle.
Carl Gassner invents the zinc-carbon battery, the first dry cell battery, making portable electronics practical.
Charles Martin Hall and independently Paul Héroult invent the Hall-Héroult process for economically producing aluminum in 1886.
Karl Benz invents the first petrol or gasoline powered auto-mobile (car).
Carl Josef Bayer invents the Bayer process for the production of alumina.
James Blyth invents the first wind turbine used for generating electricity.
John Stewart MacArthur, working in collaboration with brothers Dr. Robert and Dr. William Forrest, develops the process of gold cyanidation.
John J. Loud invents the ballpoint pen.
Thomas Edison and William Kennedy Dickson invent the Kinetoscope.
The first practical pneumatic tire was made by Scotsman John Boyd Dunlop, the patent was from 1847 by Robert William Thomson
Frédéric Swarts invents the first chlorofluorocarbons to be applied as refrigerant.
Robert Gair invents the pre-cut cardboard box.
Thomas Ahearn invents the electric oven.
John Froelich invented the gas-powered tractor
Rudolf Diesel invents the diesel engine (although Herbert Akroyd Stuart had experimented with compression ignition before Diesel).

William Stewart Halsted, invents the rubber glove for his wife Caroline Hampton as he noticed her hands were affected by the daily surgeries she had performed. The gloves were intended to prevent medical staff from developing dermatitis from surgical chemicals. The first modern disposable glove was created by Ansell Rubber Co. Pty. Ltd. in 1965.
Guglielmo Marconi invents the radio, a system of wireless communication using radio waves.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen invented the first radiograph (X-ray).

Surgical masks made of cloth were developed in Europe by physicians Jan Mikulicz-Radecki at the University of Breslau and Paul Berger in Paris, as a result of increasing awareness of germ theory and the importance of antiseptic procedures in medicine.
Hans von Pechmann synthesizes polyethylene, now the most common plastic in the world.
Waldemar Jungner invents the rechargeable nickel-cadmium battery (NiCd) as well as the nickel-iron electric storage battery (NiFe) and the rechargeable alkaline silver-cadmium battery (AgCd)
The first motorized cleaner using suction, a powered "vacuum cleaner", is patented independently by Hubert Cecil Booth and David T. Kenney.
The first successful gas turbine is invented by Ægidius Elling.
The first successful controlled powered flights of a heavier than air vehicle are made by Wilbur and Orvile Wright
The Fleming valve, the first vacuum tube and diode, is invented by John Ambrose Fleming.
Leo Baekeland invents bakelite,  the first plastic made from synthetic components.
The tuyères thermopropulsives after 1945 (Maurice Roy (fr)) known as the statoreacteur a combustion subsonique (the ramjet), R. Lorin
Cellophane is invented by Jacques E. Brandenberger.
Fritz Haber invents the Haber process.
The cloud chamber, the first particle detector, is invented by Charles Thomson Rees Wilson.
The Bergius process is developed by Friedrich Bergius.
The Kaplan turbine is invented by Viktor Kaplan.
Harry Brearley invents a process to create Martensitic stainless steel, initially labelled Rustless Steel, later marketed as Staybrite, and AISI Type 420.

The first operational military tanks are designed in Great Britain and France. They are used in battle from 1916 and 1917 respectively. The designers in Great Britain are Walter Wilson and William Tritton and in France, Eugène Brillié. (Although it is known that vehicles incorporating at least some of the features of the tank were designed in a number of countries from 1903 onward, none reached a practical form.)
The Czochralski process, widely used for the production of single crystal silicon, is invented by Jan Czochralski.
The crystal oscillator is invented by Alexander M. Nicolson using a crystal of Rochelle Salt although his priority was disputed by Walter Guyton Cady.
The Fischer-Tropsch process is developed by Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch at the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Kohlenforschung.

The Yagi-Uda Antenna or simply Yagi Antenna is invented by Shintaro Uda of Tohoku Imperial University, assisted by his colleague Hidetsugu Yagi. The Yagi Antenna was widely used during World War II. After the war they saw extensive development as home television antennas.
Robert H. Goddard launches the first liquid fueled rocket.
Harry Ferguson, patents the Three-point hitch equipment linkage system for tractors.
John Logie Baird demonstrates the world's first live working television system.
The quartz clock is invented by Warren Marrison and J.W. Horton at Bell Telephone Laboratories.

Penicillin is first observed to exude antibiotic substances by Nobel laureate Alexander Fleming. Development of medicinal penicillin is attributed to a team of medics and scientists including Howard Walter Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley.
Frank Whittle formally submitted his ideas for a turbo-jet engine. In October 1929, he developed his ideas further. On 16 January 1930, Whittle submitted his first patent (granted in 1932).
Philo Farnsworth demonstrates the first practical electronic television to the press.
The ball screw is invented by Rudolph G. Boehm.
The Supersonic combusting ramjet, Frank Whittle.[citation needed]
The Phase-contrast microscopy is invented by Frits Zernike.
The electron microscope is invented by Ernst Ruska.
FM radio is patented by inventor Edwin H. Armstrong.
Harry C. Jennings Sr. and Herbert Everest, both mechanical engineers, invented the first lightweight, steel, folding, portable wheelchair with their "X-brace" design.
Nylon, the first fully synthetic fiber is produced by Wallace Carothers while working at DuPont.
Z1, built by Konrad Zuse, is the first freely programmable computer in the world.

Nuclear fission discovered in experiment by chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann and physicists Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch. The German nuclear energy project was based on this research. The Tube Alloys project and, subsequently, the Manhattan Project and the Soviet atomic bomb project were influenced by this research.
G. S. Yunyev or Naum Gurvich invented the electric current defibrillator
John Vincent Atanasoff invented the first electronic digital computer

Pu-239 isotope (isotope of plutonium) a form of matter existing with the capacity for use as a destructive element (because the isotope has an exponentially increasing spontaneous fissile decay) within nuclear devices, Glenn Seaborg.
John Randall and Harry Boot would develop the high power, microwave generating, cavity magnetron, later applied to commercial Radar and Microwave oven appliances.
Polyester is invented by John Rex Whinfield and James Dickson.
The V-2 rocket, the world's first long range ballistic missile, developed by engineer Wernher von Braun.
Enrico Fermi developed the nuclear reactor and created the first controlled nuclear chain reaction
The non-infectious viral vaccine is perfected by Dr. Jonas Salk and Thomas Francis.
The atomic bomb is developed by the Manhattan Project and swiftly used in August 1945 in the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Percy Spencer, while employed at Raytheon, would patent a magnetron based microwave oven.

Willard Libby began his work on radiocarbon dating. He published his paper in 1946, a second paper in Science in 1947. Libby and James Arnold succeeded with the radiocarbon dating theory after results were published in Science in December 1949.
James Martin invents the ejector seat, inspired by the death of his friend and test pilot Captain Valentine Baker in an aeroplane crash in 1942.
Holography is invented by Dennis Gabor.
Floyd Farris and J.B. Clark (Stanolind Oil and Gas Corporation) invents hydraulic fracturing technology.
The first transistor, a bipolar point-contact transistor, is invented by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain under the supervision of William Shockley at Bell Labs.
Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey
The first atomic clock is developed at the National Bureau of Standards.

Basic oxygen steelmaking is developed by Robert Durrer. The majority of steel manufactured in the world is produced using the basic oxygen furnace; in 2000, it accounted for 60% of global steel output.
Bertie the Brain, debatably the first video game, is displayed to the public at the Canadian National Exhibition.
The Toroidal chamber with axial magnetic fields (the Tokamak) is developed by Igor E. Tamm and Andrei D. Sakharov.
The float glass process is developed by Alastair Pilkington.
The first thermonuclear weapon is developed.
The first video tape recorder, a helical scan recorder, is invented by Norikazu Sawazaki.

Invention of the solar battery by Bell Telephone scientists, Calvin Souther Fuller, Daryl Chapin and Gerald Pearson capturing the Sun's power. First practical means of collecting energy from the Sun and turning it into a current of electricity.
The hovercraft is patented by Christopher Cockerell.
Jonas Salk received the license for his inactivated polio vaccine
The intermodal container is developed by Malcom McLean.
The hard disk drive is invented by IBM.
The Logic Theorist computer program, the first "artificial intelligence program", was written and invented by Allen Newell, Herbert A. Simon, and Cliff Shaw.
The laser and optical amplifier are invented and named by Gordon Gould and Charles Townes. The laser and optical amplifier are foundational to powering the Internet.
The first personal computer used by one person and controlled by a keyboard, the IBM 610, is invented by IBM.
The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, is launched.
The integrated circuit is independently invented by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce.

The MOSFET (MOS transistor) is invented by the Egyptian Mohamed Atalla and the Korean Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs. It is used in almost all modern electronic products. It was smaller, faster, more reliable and cheaper to manufacture than earlier bipolar transistors, leading to a revolution in computers, controls and communication.
Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey
The first combined oral contraceptive pill becomes publicly available.
The first functioning laser is invented by Theodore Maiman.
The first electronic cigarette is created by Herbert A. Gilbert. Hon Lik is often credited with its invention as he developed the modern electronic cigarette and was the first to commercialize it.
Shinkansen, the first high-speed rail commercial passenger service.
Kevlar is invented by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont.
E. A. Johnson of the Royal Radar Establishment developed the capacitive touch display or touchscreen

The NPL network followed by the ARPANET implement packet switching for data communication, drawing on the concepts and designs of Donald Davies, and Paul Baran. These are considered precursors to the modern Internet.

Public-key cryptography is invented and developed by James H. Ellis, Clifford Cocks, Malcolm J. Williamson, Whitfield Diffie, Martin Hellman, Ralph Merkle, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman, et al.

The first single-chip microprocessor, the Intel 4004, is invented. Its development was led by Federico Faggin, using his silicon-gate MOS technology. This led to the personal computer (PC) revolution.
The first space station, Salyut 1, is launched.
IBM developed and released the world's first floppy disk and disk drive.
The first video game console, used primarily for playing video games on a TV, is the Magnavox Odyssey.
Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen developed genetic modification when they successfully modified DNA
The first fiber optic communication systems were developed by Optelecom.
The first commercial graphical user interface is introduced in 1973 on the Xerox Alto. The modern GUI is later popularized by the Xerox Star and Apple Lisa.
The first capacitive touchscreen is developed at CERN.
The Transmission Control Program is proposed by Vinton Cerf and Robert E. Kahn, building on the work of other Internet pioneers, creating the basis for the modern Internet.

The lithium-ion battery is invented by M. Stanley Whittingham, and further developed in the 1980s and 1990s by John B. Goodenough, Rachid Yazami and Akira Yoshino. It has impacted modern consumer electronics and electric vehicles.
The Rubik's cube is invented by Ernő Rubik which went on to be the best selling puzzle ever.
First general purpose home automation network technology, X10, was developed
Dr Walter Gilbert and Frederick Sanger invented a new DNA sequencing method for which they won the Nobel Prize.
The first self-driving car that did not rely upon rails or wires under the road is designed by the Tsukuba Mechanical Engineering Laboratory.
The Global Positioning System (GPS) enters service. While not the first Satellite navigation system, it is the first to enter widespread civilian use
Birth of the first child through in vitro fertilization (IVF), based on the research of  Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards
The first handheld game console with interchangeable game cartridges, the Microvision is released.
Nippon Telegraph and Telephone (NTT) launched the first cellular network in Japan.
Public dialup information, messaging and e-commerce services, were pioneered through CompuServe and RadioShack's MicroNET, and the UK's Post Office Telecommunications Prestel services.
Flash memory (both NOR and NAND types) was invented by Fujio Masuoka while working for Toshiba. It was introduced to the public in 1984.

Scientists Mark Skolnick, Ron Davis, Ray White, and David Botstein published their findings on a gene mapping tool using Restriction Fragment-length Polymorphisms (RFLP), that would have applications to identify heritable disorders, including some forms of cancer.
The first reusable spacecraft, the Space Shuttle undergoes test flights ahead of full operation in 1982
Kane Kramer develops the credit card-sized, IXI digital media player.
Televerket, a Swedish state-owned corporation, launched the Nordic Mobile Telephone (NMT) system.

Comvik, a Swedish telecommunications company, launched the first commercial automatic cellular system. However, according to the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority, the company launched an unlicensed automatic system. Comvik didn't receive a license to operate until December 1981, two months after the NMT system was launched.

A CD-ROM contains data accessible to, but not writable by, a computer for data storage and music playback. The 1985 Yellow Book standard developed by Sony and Philips adapted the format to hold any form of binary data.
Direct to home satellite television transmission, with the launch of Sky One service.
The first laptop computer is launched, the 8/16-bit Epson HX-20.
Stereolithography is invented by Chuck Hull.
Ameritech, now known as AT&T, commercialized the Bell System (its cellular network) in Chicago, Ill.
The first commercially available cell phone in the US, the DynaTAC 8000X, is created by Motorola.
Chuck Hull patents the stereolithography (SLA) process, also known as 3D printing
DNA profiling is pioneered by Alec Jeffreys.
Technophone, a British mobile phone company, created the first pocket-sized cell phone, the Excell PCT105.
Karlheinz Brandenburg would publish the audio compression algorithms that would be standardised as the: MPEG-1, layer 3 (mp3), and later the MPEG-2, layer 7 Advanced Audio Compression (AAC).
The World Wide Web is invented by computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee.
The first search engine, "Archie", was created by Alan Emtage, Bill Heelan, and Peter J. Deutsch at McGill University
The first commercial flash-based solid-state drive is launched by SunDisk.
The first sim card is developed by Munich smart-card maker Giesecke & Devrient
IBM Simon, the world's first smartphone, is developed by IBM. It had a touchscreen and the first built-in apps for a mobile device.
First generation of Bluetooth is developed by Ericsson Mobile. A form of data communication on short distances between electronic devices
A Tetris variant on the Hagenuk MT-2000 device becomes the first mobile game
DVD is an optical disc storage format, invented and developed by Philips, Sony, Toshiba, and Panasonic. DVDs offer higher storage capacity than compact discs while having the same dimensions.
The Ciena Corporation, in partnership with Sprint, deployed the first commercial dense wavelength-division multiplexing system, which created the massive capacity of the Internet.
Mobile web was first commercially offered in Finland on the Nokia 9000 Communicator phone, and it was also the first phone with texting
Bolt and Six Degrees (1997) both become the first social media sites.
Myriad Genetics released the BRACAnalysis, the first commercial genetic test for assessing the risk of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
The first capsule endoscopy was performed, after being invented in the mid-1990s by Gavriel Iddan
The first digital video recorder (DVR), the TiVo, is launched
NTT DoCoMo launches i-mode, the first integrated Online App store for mobile phones
The Food and Drug Administration approved the first contraceptive patch
Wikipedia is launched by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger as a open-content online encyclopedia
Programmer Jonathon Abrams launches Friendster, establishing the modern template for web-based social networking
Development of the Android operating system for mobile devices
First podcast, invented by Adam Curry and Dave Winer
YouTube, the first popular video-streaming site, was founded by Jawed Karim
First Kindle e-reader introduced by Amazon
The first quantum machine was created by Aaron D. O'Connell
The first synthetic organism, Mycoplasma laboratorium is created by the J. Craig Venter Institute
The first known "NFT", Quantum, was created by Kevin McCoy and Anil Dash in May.
First successful launch of a multi-use rocket by SpaceX
IBM launches IBM Q System One, its first integrated quantum computing system for commercial use.
OpenAI demonstrated an Artificial Intelligence model called GPT-3. The program was created to generate human-like responses when given prompts.
